rules: National Polygon data can contain overlaps, gaps, slivers and underlaps; not every topological anomaly is an error.
Technical overlapping polygons can arise from mapping inconsistencies and do not necessarily represent a real conflict between registered titles.
Actual overlaps are cases where two or more registered titles include the same land or property and are resolved on application.
In National Polygon quality guidance, topology describes how polygons relate to and interact with one another.
HM Land Registry states that National Polygon public data is intended to be accurate but is not guaranteed error-free or fit for every purpose.
The title plan and register record the general position of registered boundaries unless a boundary has been formally determined as exact.
The Title Number/UPRN Look Up dataset covers registered properties in England and Wales that are associated with an address containing a UPRN.
HM Land Registry records addresses when property is registered.
HM Land Registry links registration addresses to Ordnance Survey AddressBase data where possible.
When an address cannot be linked to the national address source, HM Land Registry can create its own address record.
HM Land Registry later matches its created addresses and title numbers to new AddressBase addresses when those become available.
A title number and UPRN are linked only where a relationship can be made between the AddressBase address and the title number.
In the Title Number/UPRN dataset, Title_No is a mandatory Character field.
In the Title Number/UPRN dataset, UPRN is a mandatory Integer field identifying a spatial address.
Address matching can create duplicate LRPG addresses when supplied address information does not match the Land Registry Property Gazetteer.
One duplicate-address failure mode is one LRPG address carrying a title number without a UPRN while another carries the UPRN without the title number.
An address can exist with a UPRN but no associated title number when it is not present in the Land Registry Property Gazetteer.
Some Post Office addresses excluded from AddressBase have no UPRN and therefore cannot appear in the Title Number/UPRN dataset.
HM Land Registry creates the LRPG title-to-address association when a property is registered.
When one title affects many properties, all affecting UPRNs may be associated with that title.
If an AddressBase address has not been transferred into LRPG, a title can lack a UPRN even when a UPRN exists externally.
HM Land Registry refreshes LRPG from an AddressBase change-only update on a six-week cycle.
Title Number/UPRN data may change several times during a six-week cycle, while the published dataset shows only the last change made.
The Title Descriptor class of title records the Registrar's confidence in the ownership evidence established at registration.
A single title number can have only one class of title.
HM Land Registry documents three classes of title for freehold land and four classes for leasehold land.
Absolute is the best class of title in Title Descriptor guidance.
A qualified title may be granted where a specific defect in title exists and that defect is recorded in the register.
A possessory title can be granted where title is based on adverse possession or where title deeds have been lost or destroyed.
A good leasehold title may be granted where HM Land Registry lacks evidence of the landlord's right to grant the lease.
The Planning Data entity endpoint requires the output extension to be one of json, html or geojson.
For a single-entity request, the entity path parameter is an integer entity identifier.
The Planning Data dataset-list endpoint supports json or html output.
The Planning Data single-dataset endpoint supports json or html output.
The entity-search longitude parameter requires latitude to be supplied as well.
The entity-search latitude parameter requires longitude to be supplied as well.
The entity-search geometry parameter accepts one or more geometries supplied in Well-Known Text.
The entity-search geometry_reference parameter can use the geometries of entities matching supplied references.
The entity-search geometry_curie parameter can use the geometries of entities matching supplied CURIEs.
The entity-search quality parameter can filter results by quality classification.
When both field and exclude_field are supplied, Planning Data documents that field takes precedence.
Planning Data's quality process checks for invalid dates in source data.
Planning Data's quality process checks for geometries that fall outside administrative boundaries.
Planning Data's quality process identifies duplicate entities that need reconciliation.
Planning Data states an aim to provide datasets from authoritative sources covering the entirety of England.
Defra's Data Services Platform is moving elevation delivery toward open standards rather than Esri Image Services.
Environment Agency elevation image services are being replaced by equivalent WCS and WMS services.
Environment Agency guidance distinguishes WMS as a summarised view of elevation data and WCS as the service that provides elevation values.
Current LIDAR Composite service endpoints remove the release-year suffix so the endpoint can remain persistent across future updates.
The documented persistent WCS route for the 1m LIDAR Composite DTM is lidar-composite-digital-terrain-model-dtm-1m/wcs.
Environment Agency's documented WCS example uses WCS version 2.0.1.
A direct request to the current 1m DTM WCS GetCapabilities route reached an XML response path in this session, but the browsing client could not render application/xml.
Environment Agency LIDAR specifications require absolute height error to be less than plus or minus 15 centimetres RMSE.
The documented LIDAR RMSE compares Ground Truth Survey observations with the LIDAR data.
Environment Agency expects relative height error, described as random error, to be no more than plus or minus 5 centimetres.
Ground-truth results for individual Environment Agency surveys are associated with the LIDAR Capture Programme.
Environment Agency's survey catalogue states that it holds survey data for England.
The survey catalogue states that if no data is listed for a location, the Environment Agency has not surveyed that location to date.
Environment Agency survey products are supplied in 5km tiles aligned to the Ordnance Survey grid.
Survey tile naming can encode the unique survey identifier, OS grid reference, start date flown and end date flown.
Environment Agency surface-model products are supplied as GeoTIFF raster data.
Environment Agency point-cloud products are supplied in LAZ, the compressed form of LAS.
Environment Agency point-cloud returns are classified into ground, low vegetation, medium vegetation and high vegetation classes.
An Environment Agency Digital Surface Model contains ground and surface objects and is created from the last or only LIDAR pulse returned to the sensor.
An Environment Agency Digital Terrain Model uses last-return points classified as ground and filters out surface objects.
Manual editing of the derived Environment Agency DTM means classified ground points in the point cloud need not exactly match the final DTM.
Time-stamped point-cloud data is organised in 5km download zip files for each year of survey.
The size of a time-stamped point-cloud tile depends on the spatial resolution of the source data.
Environment Agency coverage metadata records the start and end dates flown for a survey.
Environment Agency coverage metadata can include the average point density of a point-cloud component.
The current Time Stamped DTM metadata identifier is dbadf364-0192-4bcf-a223-f3d403f08682.
The current Time Stamped DTM metadata reports a revision date of 19 July 2024.
The current Time Stamped DTM metadata period extends through 18 April 2024.
The Time Stamped DTM metadata gives its coordinate reference system as EPSG:27700.
The Time Stamped DTM metadata exposes an OSGM02-to-OSGM15 adjustment-grid support resource.
OS Terrain 50 ASCII grid is a generic text-based DTM format also known as ArcInfo ASCII grid or ArcGrid ASCII.
Ordnance Survey states that standard GIS software can read the ASCII grid without additional translation.
OS Terrain 50 grid supply provides ASCII grid data alongside a GML file.
In gridded supply, the GML file provides metadata such as location, grid spacing and the vertical reference system.
The grid GML also carries spatial-reference information in a software-independent form.
OS Terrain 50 ASCII rows are ordered from west to east.
Each OS Terrain 50 ASCII tile has 200 pixels per row.
Each OS Terrain 50 grid pixel represents 50 metres by 50 metres.
Successive ASCII rows progress 50 metres south from the previous row.
An OS Terrain 50 ASCII tile represents a 10 kilometre by 10 kilometre raster.
OS Terrain 50 ASCII heights are encoded as real numeric values.
OS Terrain 50 ASCII height values are supplied to the nearest 0.1 metre.
The grid data file uses the <tile name>.asc naming pattern.
The companion grid GML file uses the <tile name>.gml naming pattern.
The companion projection file uses the <tile name>.prj naming pattern.
The companion Esri styling file uses the <tile name>.asc.aux.xml naming pattern.
The per-tile grid metadata file uses the Metadata_<tile name>.xml naming pattern.
The documented ASCII header declares ncols 200.
The documented ASCII header declares nrows 200.
The documented ASCII header declares cellsize 50.
OS Terrain 50 contour GML is supplied as GML 3.2.1.
Contour supply includes a per-tile metadata XML file recording information such as flying date.
OS Terrain 50 spot heights are generated by selecting the highest mass point within each closed contour.
If an automatically selected spot-height point has the same height as its contour, the point is removed.
A spot height can be lower than the surrounding contour when it represents a genuine depression.
OS Terrain 50 contour spot-height z values are rounded to zero decimal places.
OS Terrain 50 tile metadata follows the GEMINI metadata standard.
OS Terrain 50 metadata is supplied on a per-tile basis.
OS Terrain 50 tile metadata identifies the projected horizontal reference system as British National Grid.
OS Terrain 50 tile metadata identifies the vertical reference system as Ordnance Datum Newlyn using EPSG:5701.
Where a tile contains multiple flying dates, metadata records the earliest and latest flying dates present.
The earliest and latest flying dates in tile metadata are allowed to be identical.
OS Terrain 50 metadata defines processing date as the date the tile was created, not the date of the real-world change or survey.
OS Terrain 50 metadata contains an incrementing version number indicating how many times the tile has been published.
OS Terrain 50 metadata distinguishes creation from revision through the reason-for-change information.
OS Terrain 50 lineage can state that a tile was created from new imagery.
OS Terrain 50 lineage can state that some parts of a tile were revised from new imagery.
OS Terrain 50 lineage can state that new imagery was examined and no change was required.
Ordnance Survey supplies an XSLT stylesheet that can transform Terrain metadata XML into HTML for easier viewing.
The Esri asc.aux.xml styling file contains min, max, mean and standard-deviation height statistics intended for display styling.
The same asc.aux.xml styling statistics are supplied for every tile, so they are not candidate-specific elevation measurements.
OS Terrain 50 contours are supplied as a single national GeoPackage file.
The Terrain 50 GeoPackage contains spot_height, land_water_boundary and contour_line layers.
Current GeoPackage attribute naming uses user-friendly snake_case names such as property_value, spot_height_type, water_level_category and contour_line_type.
OS Terrain 50 contour vector tiles are supplied as a single national MBTiles file in Web Mercator EPSG:3857.
